Jyoti had promised Maa on Chhath morning, her hand on his head: no more drinking. He meant it. He lasted four days. By the fifth evening the pull was louder than the promise, and he was behind the grain godown with the older boys again.
Now the consequences kept coming. His B.Com marks sheet from the college in Siwan showed two backlogs. Rehana, who ran the tuition centre where he taught maths in the evenings, had called him in on Monday. "Late three times, and once you smelt of it in front of the children. I can't keep you, Jyoti." He had nodded, face hot, unable to argue.
Tonight he sat on the canal bridge with an empty bottle at his feet, counting the promises he'd broken this year. He had tried cutting down to weekends, then to festivals only. Every plan had lasted less than a week. He felt like a rat in a drum, running and getting nowhere.

qa.q: How many backlogs did Jyoti's B.Com marks sheet show?
qa.a: Two backlogs.

qa.q: How does Jyoti feel on the canal bridge, and what shows it?
qa.a: He feels ashamed and trapped; he counts his broken promises and feels like a rat in a drum, running and getting nowhere.

qa.q: What turning point is still open to Jyoti at this stage?
qa.a: Since cutting down alone keeps failing, he could tell Maa the whole truth and go with her to a doctor or de-addiction centre for proper help.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Rehana to let Jyoti go?
qa.a: Rehana had to protect the children, but letting go of a teacher who came late and smelt of alcohol may have felt sad and uncomfortable, especially seeing him unable to argue.

grounding: Shows a young man's drinking costing him marks and a job, failed attempts to cut down, and a sincere promise to his mother broken within days.

passage:
Zanele had set the timer for two hours. She had set it every night that week, and every night she had switched it off and played on until the birds started in the jacaranda outside her Johannesburg residence window.
Now the consequences were arriving all at once. An email from her tutor: three missed tutorials, final warning. A bookshop shift lost because she slept through it. And Omar on the phone that afternoon, tired rather than angry: "I don't know how to be with someone who's always somewhere else."
At Easter she had promised her mother, crying, that this term would be different. She had meant every word.
Tonight she deleted the game, then sat on her bed for twenty minutes before reinstalling it, hating herself the whole time. The shame only made her want to disappear into it more.

qa.q: How long did Zanele set the timer for each night?
qa.a: Two hours.

qa.q: Why did Zanele reinstall the game while hating herself?
qa.a: The craving was stronger than her sincere wish to stop, and the shame of failing again made her want to escape into the game even more.

qa.q: What could Zanele do now that cutting down on her own keeps failing?
qa.a: She could tell someone safe, like her mother or Omar, and reach out to the university counselling service or a doctor for proper help instead of relying on timers.

qa.q: What is Omar experiencing in the relationship right now?
qa.a: Omar sounds tired rather than angry, feeling alone because Zanele is 'always somewhere else' and unsure how to stay close.

grounding: Illustrates gaming costing a student her tutorials, a job shift and closeness in a relationship, with failed cut-downs and a broken promise to her mother.

Student counsellor's note, 18 February
Nandini, second-year commerce, came in today after her tutor raised concerns. Her attendance has dropped to half. She lost her part-time job at the bookshop last month for missing shifts. She told me her relationship ended in January.
She said she has tried to cut down on drinking three times since Diwali and each time it lasted only a few days. "I promised my mother on her birthday. I meant it. I broke it two days later." She cried and said she feels trapped and ashamed.
I told her this is a health problem, not a character flaw. With her agreement, I have referred her to the college doctor and a de-addiction counsellor. We meet again Friday.
Ramesh, counsellor

qa.q: What job did Nandini lose?
qa.a: Her part-time job at the bookshop.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when she described breaking her promise?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and trapped, having sincerely meant the promise but broken it under craving.

qa.q: What steps did Ramesh take, and why are they helpful?
qa.a: Ramesh called it a health problem, not a character flaw, and, with her agreement, referred her to the college doctor and a de-addiction counsellor.

qa.q: How might Nandini's mother feel about the broken promise?
qa.a: Her mother is probably hurt and frightened, perhaps unaware how hard it is to keep such a promise alone.

grounding: Shows a counsellor's note on a student whose grades, job and relationship suffer, whose attempts to cut down fail and whose promises break under craving.

Diary, 2 a.m.
I deleted the betting app again tonight. Fourth time this month. I'll reinstall it tomorrow. I always do.
Hemant left last week. He said he couldn't watch me lie about money any more. My exam results came: two backlogs. I used to be the one who topped the class.
On Sunday I promised Papa, with my hand on his shoulder, that I'd stop. He cried. I meant every word. By Tuesday night I was placing bets again, hiding under the blanket so the light wouldn't show.
I feel like I'm trapped inside something that's eating me. I'm so ashamed I can't look at myself.
I think I need real help. Not just deleting an app.
Rajni

qa.q: How many times has Rajni deleted the betting app this month?
qa.a: Four times.

qa.q: What is Rajni feeling as she writes?
qa.a: Rajni feels trapped and deeply ashamed, unable to keep a sincere promise despite meaning it.

qa.q: What turning point does Rajni reach at the end of the entry?
qa.a: Rajni recognises that deleting the app isn't enough and that real help is needed, such as a doctor or counsellor.

qa.q: What might Papa have been feeling when he cried?
qa.a: Papa was probably heartbroken and afraid for Rajni, and hopeful the promise would hold.

grounding: Shows a young person's diary about losing a relationship and slipping grades, failed attempts to stop betting and a promise broken under craving.

passage: The results list was pinned outside the college office in Bahraich, and Hafsa found her roll number in a column she had never been in before: supplementary. Rashmi squeezed her arm; Hafsa pulled away. Three weeks ago she had promised Ammi, her hand on Ammi's hand, that she had deleted the card game. She had. For four days. Then, alone on the roof one night, the itch came back so strongly that she reinstalled it before she could think. Now the fee money was gone, she had not answered Rashmi's messages in days, and every promise she made felt true when she said it and false by nightfall. Walking home past the sweet shop, Hafsa felt trapped inside her own hands.
